None of the three solutions reaches what I believe is the correct answer, so I am picking the least wrong one. My reasoning is partly from memory of the literature, not a full derivation.

**Check of A₅.** Its non-linear degrees are 3, 3, 4, 5, each with exactly one distinct prime divisor, so A₅ is in 𝒢. This gives 2, 3, 5 ∈ P.

**A missing group.** PSL(2,8) has non-linear degrees 7, 8, 9, again each a prime power. It is also in 𝒢, so 7 ∈ P. Every solution misses this.

**Why a finite sum is expected.** From memory, the known classification of non-solvable groups of this kind is very restrictive, so P should be finite, which rules out Solution 1. I did not re-derive that classification. By my recollection, P = {2, 3, 5, 7}, which would give a sum of 17.

**Evaluating the solutions.**
- **Solution 1** claims P is all primes and answers ∞. It is wrong, since the class is highly restrictive.
- **Solution 2** answers 5 from P = {2, 3}. It wrongly ignores the degree 5 of A₅, so it is wrong.
- **Solution 3** answers 10 from P = {2, 3, 5}. It correctly uses A₅'s full set of degrees but misses PSL(2,8), so it is also wrong, though it is the closest.

CHOICE: 3
